sources.title: Human History Map, imported Athabaskan and Athabascan records
sources.note: Current local index and all 15 matching border features decoded. athabaskan 800-1700, with seam 1492-1500 absent; athabascan indexed 1600-1800 but geometry begins 1700. Adjacent 1650 and 1700 shapes have common bounds and 92.59% intersection/union of quarter-degree test-grid points; not geometrically identical. After 1783 it contracts to Alaska.

sources.title: University of Alaska Fairbanks, About the Dene/Athabaskan Languages Conference
sources.note: Direct institutional page read: language-family extent, alternative spellings, local preference for Dene versus Athabaskan, and Gallatin 1826 naming. Language-family relationship does not imply one state or one collective ethnic identity.

sources.title: P. Gregory Hare and colleagues, Ethnographic and Archaeological Investigations of Alpine Ice Patches in Southwest Yukon, Canada (2004)
sources.note: Original Arctic 57(3):260-272 PDF directly read. Pages 260-262 community context/hunting sites, 267-270 arrows and material technology, page 261 youth science camps. Radiocarbon dates explicitly uncalibrated; no arithmetic conversion to exact calendar dates. Earlier artifacts not equated to a named modern nation.

sources.title: Parks Canada, Yukon Ice Patches
sources.note: Original institutional description read in indexed source: 7500-year record, rare organic preservation, Carcross/Tagish and Yukon Government collaboration, melting and intergenerational research. Long chronology treated as prehistory before this atlas interval, not an 800 CE founding.

sources.title: Brian Fagan, Where We Found a Whale: A History of Lake Clark National Park and Preserve (2008)
sources.note: Original NPS book directly read, Chapter 8: printed pages 107-108 houses/trade, page 110 kinship, leaders and teaching. These are historically reconstructed/ethnographically documented Dena’ina practices, not dated archaeological statements for all northern language communities. No universal gender or shaman claims used.

sources.title: Karen K. Gaul, Nanutset: An Ethnohistory of Lake Clark National Park and Preserve (2007)
sources.note: Original NPS report directly read. Printed page 53 Tyonek post and 1797 destruction; pages 91-92 fish storage; pages 103-104 birch-bark containers; page 133 Mary Hobson 1985 remembered wound treatments. Later oral accounts dated as later witnesses. Whole 196-page PDF one attribution budget.

sources.title: Douglas R. Reger and Charles M. Mobley, Dena’ina Use of Marine Resources for Food and Tools (2008)
sources.note: Original Alaska Journal of Anthropology 6(1-2):199-210 PDF read, pages 204-206 KEN-360 1500-1650 houses and bark-lined tool cache. The approximate Kasilof point lies inside the later outline; Kenai modern examples farther north lie outside. General ethnographic/archaeological identification criteria and material limits read.

sources.title: National Park Service, Kijik Archeological District National Historic Landmark
sources.note: Direct official page read, updated 16 October 2024. District contains houses, steam baths, underground caches, community houses and later Russian Orthodox church. Early twentieth-century disease/relocation and continued family harvest visits supported. Individual structures not all dated before contact.

sources.title: Kenaitze Indian Tribe, Mission, vision and traditional values
sources.note: Direct official tribal page read; exact written Chiqinik and translation thank you under Values. Also independently checked indexed Tribal Research Ordinance 2016-03, printed page 7, adopted 15 July 2016, which lists the same word/gloss. Direct ordinance PDF has no extractable text; main readable tribal page used. Modern Roman orthography, not a medieval inscription.

sources.title: Kenaitze Indian Tribe, Annual Report 2022
sources.note: Direct original tribal annual report read: Message from Chair, PDF page 7/printed page 8, and Education PDF page 18/printed page 19. Learning campus and early-learning programs reported for 2022. This is a specific modern nation and a comparison beyond the atlas outline, not one polity encompassing all Athabascan speakers.

proposedOverrides.name: Athabascan
proposedOverrides.summary: A later atlas spelling for the same broad northern language-family umbrella; communities remain distinct.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Share one carefully phased umbrella narrative, preserving both original index intervals. UAF explicitly documents alternative spellings; atlas geometry is successive and substantially overlapping, not exactly identical.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Early Canada-centered bbox [-141.134,52.413,-111.495,64.835]. After 1530 extends to Alaska bbox [-161.003,52.412,-111.373,70.206]. 1650 versus 1700 common bbox; quarter-degree grid overlap 4462/4819 union points (92.59%). Athabascan first feature starts 1700 despite indexed 1600. Final 1783-1800 feature contracts to Alaska.
batchIdentityNotes.limits: No actual mass migration, conquest, or ethnic border inferred from map changes. Earlier record has a 1492-1500 seam gap. Modern Kenai examples beyond the omitted coastal outline are explicit comparisons; the approximate Kasilof point is inside later outlines. Modern Kenaitze not claimed as part of every earlier outline.
batchIdentityNotes.exclusions: No aliases for Navajo, Apache, Diné Bikéyah, separate Dene nations, Eyak, Tlingit, Haida or neighboring Inuit/Yupik peoples. Tlingit participants in shared Yukon research do not become Athabascan by association.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Local archaeological cases distinguished from historical reconstructions and twentieth-/twenty-first-century oral/printed witnesses. Uncalibrated Yukon radiocarbon dates not converted to exact calendar years. No invented exact item-year metadata.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Chiqinik / thank you, official Kenaitze values page and independently indexed 2016 ordinance. Modern Dena’ina orthography and specific community explicitly identified.
